name: Murinbata
confidence_why: Mansfield's 2019 grammar, building on his 2017 acoustic study, finds no metrical word stress in Murrinhpatha but only a pitch accent on the penultimate syllable of the phrase-final prosodic word, whereas the older impressionistic descriptions of Walsh 1976, Street and Mollinjin 1981 and Blythe 2009 place primary stress on the first syllable and disagree with one another about secondary stresses.

new_statements.quote: In longer polysynthetic verbs, the coverb generally attracts primary stress. In careful speech there may also be some secondary stress on the first syllable of the verb. Thus a verb like wurdamninthardarrerndernwarda could be expected to have the following stress pattern, wùrdamninthardarrérndernwarda. However in the conversational data, it is unusual to find verbs bearing more than a single stressed syllable. (p. 264) | Both of these words normally bear stress on the first syllable (Thúykem, wúlgumen). (p. 271) | The word thamuny (here pronounced thaminy), “maternal grandfather”, ordinarily attracts stress on the first syllable. (p. 17)

new_statements.rule_in_words: No phonology chapter (the thesis is a conversation-analytic study of person reference), but the stress facts are stated incidentally and explicitly: simple words (nominals, kin terms, address terms: thámuny, Thúykem, wúlgumen; p. 17, p. 271, p. 276 n. 244, p. 287 'their expected first-syllable stress patterns') bear stress on the first syllable; in long polysynthetic verbs the coverb (lexical stem) attracts primary stress, with at most a secondary stress on the verb's first syllable (p. 264). Footnote 234 (p. 263) adds that Murriny Patha is 'a syllable-timed language rather than a stress-timed language' and that 'in conversation polysynthetic verbs generally have just one stressed syllable (at most two)'. The transcription conventions in the front matter mark stress by underlining (Jefferson-style), not as a rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'In careful speech there may also be some secondary stress on the first syllable of the verb' (p. 264), e.g. wùrdamninthardarrérndernwarda; in conversational data verbs rarely bear more than one stressed syllable (p. 263 n. 234, p. 264). Ch. 6 p. 126 n. 120 gives a phonetic correlate: 'a tendency to voice stops that form the onset of stressed syllables and to devoice the onsets of unstressed syllables, though this is by no means universal.'
new_statements.exceptions: Speakers deliberately shift the pitch peak off the normally stressed first syllable onto the next syllable as a discourse device (prosodic 'tweaking' of referential items and vocatives: pp. 17, 271-272, 276 n. 244, 287). A barely perceptible nominal classifier ku preceding the verb can suppress the verb-initial secondary stress (p. 264). Statements are about Wadeye conversational speech, not a controlled phonological description.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Murrinh-Patha as spoken at Wadeye (Port Keats), NT; Blythe's data are the Murriny Patha Song Project conversational corpus (2004-2008 recordings, Song Project orthography with four vowels and 24 consonants), Nordlinger's are her Wadeye fieldnotes. 'Murinbata' in the catalog is the older spelling of the same language (glottocode murr1258); no distinct dialect is at issue.

readall_conflicts: Between the two listed works there is no conflict (Nordlinger is silent). But Blythe's initial-stress statements sit alongside two sources already held by the project in the same check folder from an earlier reading (not in this works list): Street & Mollinjin 1981 (WP-A-5, pp. 206-209) say stress is non-phonemic, primary on the first syllable of one- to three-syllable words (three-syllable words add a secondary on the final: 'la.ma."ta 'shoulder'), first and third syllables in four- and five-syllable words, with alternative patterns (secondary initial, primary on the second) in some polymorphemic verbs; this agrees with Blythe's first-syllable nominals and with his 'stress varies by verb structure' picture. Mansfield 2019 (Murrinhpatha Morphology and Phonology, pp. 86-87), however, analyses prominence as a single pitch accent per prosodic phrase anchored on the PENULTIMATE syllable of the right-most prosodic word (kaɖíɾak 'eyebrow', malkimáɾin 'vein'); for disyllables that coincides with Blythe (Thúykem, thámuny) and for four-syllable words with Street & Mollinjin's 'first and third', but for trisyllables it contradicts Blythe's wúlgumen and Street & Mollinjin's 'la.ma."ta. Blythe's coverb-attracts-primary-stress rule for polysynthetic verbs is a morphological condition that neither the initial nor the penultimate account states as such. So the field disagrees on the default position (initial vs penultimate/PWord-based) and on whether the phenomenon is stress or pitch accen…

sources.quote: 'Stress in Murinbata is non-phonemic. There are three degrees of stress, namely: primary stress, secondary stress and non-stressed. None of these stress types occur adjacent to themselves, except in the case of reduplication.' Monomorphemic: 'Two syllable words ...: primary stress occurs on the first syllable'; 'Three syllable monomorphemic words: primary stress occurs on the initial syllable and secondary stress occurs on the final syllable' ['la.ma."ta] 'shoulder'; 'Four syllable words, monomorphemic and polymorphemic: primary stress occurs on the first and third syllables' ['wa.lu.'mu.ma];
